abstract.p: Transcript of a Lecture by Paul Tillich by Peter H. John

this idea has consequences today in every philosophical discussion. This weekend I was in Washington
and had to give several lectures, two of them under the title “Psychoanalysis and Religion”
and “Existentialism and Psychoanalysis”.This probably refers to Paul Tillich, Psychoanalysis and Christianity, a lecture given at the Washington School of Psychiatry, November 6, 1955, bMS 649/49 (19). In 1955 there was also published an essay: The Theological Significance of Existentialism and Psychoanalysis (Faith and Freedom 9 [Autumn 1955], 1–11, in Paul Tillich, Theology of Culture [ed. Robert C. Kimball; Oxford, 1959], 112–126). These two lectures continuously came to a point
which later on came out very clearly in the discussion, that the fundamental decision about existentialism
is a decision about the Christian doctrine of creation, whether the world is distorted in its not only
existential nature (which also is the Christian doctrine), but also that it is distorted in its very
nature, or in its essential nature also—which then is nothing else than its existential nature.

Now this was the real point of discussion: Is the world, in its essential structure, evil?
Or is the world, in its essential structure, good? Is Augustine right when he says “Being as being is good”
(Esse qua esse bonum est), Esse qua esse bonum est is a scholastic condensation of the Augustinian phrase in quantum sunt, bona sunt (e.g. in De natura boni c.1 [CSEL 25,2 855f.## Zycha##; PL 42,551), De vera religione 20,38 [CCSL 32, 206f.]; De civitate Dei 11,22 [#CCSL 48,340f##prüfen#]). This principle is taken up by Thomas Aquinas in Summa theologiae I, q 5, among others, relying directly on Augustin’s maxim. In Augustine’s own thought, it occurs within the context of his Privatio boni-doctrine. Tillich considers this fundamental to Christian thought, e.g. in his Berlin lecture Die menschliche Situation im Lichte der Theologie und Existentialanalyse (Freie Universität Berlin, Sommersemester 1952), 14 July, in which he emphasizes the importance of the Augustinian statement for the Christian doctrine of man, thereby highlighting the distinction from paganism, other religions, and philosophical claims such as Greek philosophy, naturalism, and existentialism: “Die einzige essential optimistische Weltanschauung ist die christliche; die griechische ist essential pessimistisch, weil im Griechentum der Gedanke der widerstrebenden Materie den Schöpfungsgedanken unmöglich macht und den augustinischen Satz ‘esse qua esse bonum est’ unmöglich macht.” (EW 16, 248f.). or is Sartre the existentialist right when he says that “man's essence is his
existence,”Sartre is credited with the characterization of existentialism—which builds on the ideas of Schelling and Kierkegaard—that “l’existence précède l’essence” (existence precedes essence). With this statement, Sartre challenges the classical philosophical view that essence is more central than existence. He uses this phrase in a lecture titled Existentialism is a Humanism (1945; published in 1946 as L’existentialisme est un humanisme). Here, Sartre modifies Heidegger’s phrase “The ‘essence’ of Dasein lies in existence” (“Das ‘Wesen’ des Daseins liegt in der Existenz”) from Being and Time § 9,1 (1927). Heidegger, however, distances himself from Sartre’s existentialism (see his famous 1947 letter Über den Humanismus to the French philosopher Jean Beaufret, in which Heidegger criticizes various historical variants and manifestations of humanism). there is nothing except his existence; and what he calls his essence is only a reflection
of his existence?—This was the point of discussion. And this is the point in which the problem of
creation becomes actual for every present-day philosophical discussion insofar as it transcends the
realm of mere logic. I am very glad for this experience I had this weekend, that this came out so
clearly in the preparation of these lectures and later in the reaction to them.
